observations.text: Main article reports random assignment to extended-release exenatide 2 mg or matching placebo weekly; defines primary composite first occurrence of cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, or nonfatal stroke; reports coprimary noninferiority/superiority hypotheses; and identifies EXSCEL as NCT01144338.
Participants were randomly assigned 1:1; the report describes computer-generated block randomization within each site, stratified by cardiovascular history.
Primary endpoint is first occurrence of cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, or nonfatal stroke in a time-to-event analysis.
Primary time-to-event analyses used Cox proportional hazards in ITT, defined as all randomized patients.
Primary ITT result: HR 0.91 (95% CI 0.83 to 1.00), noninferior for safety, not superior for efficacy.
Main article names EXSCEL ClinicalTrials.gov number NCT01144338; intake condition records registry query NCT01455896 unavailable. Identifier conflict is unresolved; no registry obtained.

considerations: Possible dependence in 3.3 does not establish likely dependence in 3.4. Judge likelihood from missingness reasons and trial circumstances; absent contrary evidence alone does not establish likelihood.

Keep the stages distinct: observed outcome data and follow-up availability describe what was obtained; 3.3 asks whether missingness could depend on the true value; 3.4 asks whether that dependence was likely. Do not promote possible dependence to likely dependence without supporting evidence.

Full guidance section 6.1, p. 39 distinguishes genuinely missing measurements (D3) from available outcomes deliberately excluded from analysis (D2). Outcome-driven rescue, switching, or post-change analysis exclusion does not by itself establish non-observation; scheduled collection does not establish observation either. Link the outcome-related reason to actual missing measurements or missing follow-up before treating it as a D3 mechanism. If that link is unknown, retain it as an unresolved premise rather than assigning analysis exclusions to missingness.

Paired control: after the same outcome-driven treatment change, endpoint measurements collected but omitted from analysis raise an assignment-analysis concern in D2; measurements not obtained require D3 appraisal. If collection is only planned or unspecified, observed availability remains unknown. Differences in rescue rates alone are not differences in missing-outcome rates. Compare post-change handling with the approved assignment target; matching endpoint and time point alone does not establish the same estimand.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.

response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

considerations: Compare actual methods and detection opportunities. Assessor awareness or possible reporting influence alone does not establish a between-group method difference; assess awareness and influence in 4.3 to 4.5.

Detection opportunity is the chance an outcome could be identified or recorded, including passive ascertainment or intervention-related visits. Keep it separate from measurement susceptibility (4.1) and from who knew the assignment (4.3).
A different visit schedule or passive collection is not enough on its own: explain how it could make the approved outcome more or less likely to be detected in one group.

Extra visits for toxicity monitoring do not establish differential measurement of mortality when death is captured through the same complete registry in both groups; those same visits may change detection of a lab-detected toxicity measured at those visits. State any mortality-specific pathway if one is supported.

For adverse events, compare the actual start and end of the AE observation window, visit schedule, post-treatment follow-up, and ascertainment method with the approved safety window. questions.decision_rule: Compare the approved Result with the applicable plan for the exact intervention comparison, cohort, endpoint, time window, population, analysis, and effect measure. Distinguish protocol or ethics approval, plan finalization, amendment effective dates, registry posting or update, data cutoff, database lock, and investigators' access to unblinded outcome data; only compare chronology when the relevant events and precision are established. Changes made before unblinded data were available, or clearly unrelated to results such as a broken machine, do not raise concerns.
evidence_needed: A sufficiently detailed protocol or SAP, its source-located chronology and finalization date relative to unblinded outcome data, and the reported analysis. Capture each dated event as reported; approval, cutoff, or database lock does not by itself establish when investigators could see unblinded outcomes.

For an original plan and an amended plan, capture the source-located content and chronology separately. An SAP embedded in a protocol, supplement, or combined document is still plan Evidence when its section and scope can be located; a separate SAP file is not required. An absent or unresolved plan remains an information limit.
questions.no_information_rule: Use a definitive answer when firm evidence establishes timing and correspondence. Use a probable answer when source facts and trial circumstances support only an inference. Use no_information when neither is supported. A plan mention or matching endpoint alone does not establish timing.

considerations: Assess correspondence between the applicable plan and the exact approved Result: outcome, time point, population, effect measure, and analysis must be compared.

Assess applicability before chronology: a platform or master plan may cover several comparisons and cohorts, so its presence does not establish applicability to the approved Result. Establish chronology separately: plan finalization must precede availability of unblinded outcome data. Protocol approval, ethics approval, amendment, initial registry posting, registry update, retrieval, data cutoff, and database lock are distinct events; none substitutes for the source-located date of plan finalization or investigator access to unblinded results.

Current registry content does not establish unseen historical intent. A data cutoff or database lock is not itself proof of when investigators accessed unblinded outcomes. Preserve unresolved applicability or chronology instead of filling the gap from report wording that merely looks prespecified.

Results-driven selection is a separate concern from whether a plan exists or whether its chronology is known. Do not infer selection merely from an amendment or from a mismatch without evidence that the choice was driven by results. Not establishing that a plan was early is not evidence that it was late: ground a negative chronology inference in source facts and trial circumstances, or preserve no_information when those cannot support a reasonable probable answer.

Neutral paired control: an applicable plan for the approved cohort differs from a platform plan for another phase; a source-located finalization date before investigator access differs from the same plan with access timing unresolved.

A plan may be an identified section of a combined protocol or supplement. Navigate to that section and retain its exact Source and page coordinates; the lack of a separately named SAP file does not show that no plan exists.

Distinguish confidential data-monitoring access from access by trial investigators making analysis decisions. Staff providing confidential data to a monitoring committee are excepted in the official guidance; that access alone does not establish late prespecification. Public interim results are different evidence. Refining an analysis with blinded data is generally acceptable unless variables reveal intervention identity.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

4|CLINICAL PROTOCOL

6|1
7|INTRODUCTION
8|1.1
9|Background
10|Type 2 diabetes mellitus is a leading public health issue. Often regarded as a mild
11|disease, it is the fourth leading cause of death in developed countries and the number of people
12|world wide with diabetes is predicted to exceed 300 million by the year 2025. Diabetes remains
13|the leading cause of blindness, end stage renal disease and lower extremity amputations and
14|confers a two to four times greater risk of heart disease and strokes.
15|The majority of people with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) die as a result of
16|cardiovascular disease (CVD). Epidemiological analysis of UKPDS data from patients with
17|newly-diagnosed T2DM showed that potentially modifiable risk factors for CVD were a raised
18|LDL cholesterol, a low HDL cholesterol, hyperglycemia, hypertension and smoking (1).
19|Elevated glucose levels were also the major determinant of microvascular complications. A
20|number of trials in people with T2DM have shown that their CVD risk can be reduced by
21|lowering LDL cholesterol (2,3), blood pressure (4,5), glycated haemoglobin (6,7) or all three risk
22|factors (8).
23|1.2
24|Rationale for Conduct of the Study
25|Exenatide, a GLP-1 receptor agonist, has been shown in randomized clinical trials to
26|improve glycemic control, augment endogenous insulin secretion, to reduce blood pressure and
27|promote weight loss with a meta-analysis of exenatide twice-daily (BYETTA) trials (9) showing
28|a trend to lower relative risk for CV events versus pooled comparators of 0.70 (95% confidence
29|interval 0.38 - 1.31). BYETTA (exenatide) injection is currently available in the US and in
30|many countries worldwide for people with type 2 diabetes who are unable to achieve good
31|glycemic control with common oral therapies. Exenatide once weekly (EQW), a new
32|formulation of exenatide that is administered once weekly rather than twice daily, is under
33|development and currently being reviewed by the US FDA.
34|In a 30-week, randomized, open-label trial, EQW treatment resulted in a significantly
35|greater improvement in glycemic control, as measured by hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c), compared to
36|7

1|EXSCEL Clinical Study Protocol BCB109
2|Page 6
3|CONFIDENTIAL
4|exenatide administered twice daily (10). Furthermore, treatment with EQW for one year (52
5|weeks) showed net reductions of 2.0% in HbA1c, 0.06 mmol/l (2.2 mg/dl) LDL cholesterol, 6
6|mmHg in systolic blood pressure and 4 kg in body weight (11). Thus, EQW represents a novel
7|therapeutic approach to the treatment of T2DM that could potentially impact the occurrence of
8|cardiovascular events in patients mediated by improvements in multiple CV risk factors, as well
9|as reducing glycemia.
10|EXSCEL (EXenatide Study of Cardiovascular Event Lowering) is a pragmatic, long-
11|term, placebo-controlled, double-blinded trial which seeks to characterize the effects of EQW on
12|cardiovascular-related outcomes in patients with type 2 diabetes when added to the current usual
13|care for glycemic control in a standard care setting.
14|2
15|STUDY OBJECTIVES AND HYPOTHESES
16|2.1
17|Primary Objective
18|The primary objective of EXSCEL will be to evaluate the effect of EQW, used in
19|conjunction with the current usual care for glycemic control, on major macrovascular events
20|when administered to patients with type 2 diabetes.
21|Objective: To compare the impact of including EQW as part of usual care vs. usual care without
22|exenatide on major CV outcomes as measured by the primary CV composite endpoint of CV-
23|related death, nonfatal myocardial infarction (MI), or nonfatal stroke.
24|Hypothesis: EQW, when used as part of usual care, is superior to usual care without exenatide
25|with regard to the risk of developing a confirmed event in the primary CV composite endpoint.
26|2.2
27|Secondary Objectives
28|The secondary objectives of EXSCEL are to evaluate the effect of EQW treatment used
29|in conjunction with the current usual care for glycemic control on:
30|(1)
31|All cause mortality
32|(2)
33|Each of the components of the primary composite CV endpoint
34|(3)
35|Hospitalization for acute coronary syndrome (ACS)
36|(4)
37|Hospitalization for heart failure (CHF)
38|

5|Additional Objectives
6|Additional objectives of EXSCEL are to evaluate the effect of EQW treatment used in
7|conjunction with the current usual care for glycemic control on:
8|(1)
9|Revascularization procedures. This will include percutaneous coronary intervention
10|with or without stenting, coronary artery bypass grafting, revascularization and/or
11|stenting for peripheral arterial disease, carotid endarterectomy, or carotid stenting.
12|(2)
13|Time to initiation of first co-interventional agent (i.e., next AHA or chronic insulin
14|therapy)
15|(3)

17|(4)

19|- HbA1c
20|- body weight
21|- blood pressure
22|- lipid profile
23|(5)
24|Quality of life assessed by the EQ-5D (EuroQol 5 Dimension) questionnaire.
25|(6)
26|Medical resource use and total direct medical costs.
27|(7)
28|Incremental cost-effectiveness analysis of exenatide once weekly as part of usual care
29|compared with usual care without exenatide.
30|3
31|TRIAL GOVERNANCE
32|EXSCEL is a multinational pragmatic trial that will be conducted in approximately 400
33|sites worldwide. It will be run jointly by the Duke Clinical Research Institute (DCRI) and the
34|University of Oxford Diabetes Trials Unit (DTU) Academic Research Organizations (AROs), in
35|an academic collaboration with Amylin Pharmaceuticals Inc. (Amylin). EXSCEL will be Co-
36|Chaired by Professors Robert Califf (Cardiologist) and Rury Holman (Endocrinologist) but
37|sponsored and funded by Amylin on behalf of the Alliance (Amylin & Eli Lilly).
38|The EXSCEL Executive Committee (EC) will have overall responsibility for the
39|oversight and management of the trial (Figure 1). The EC will consist of approximately eleven
40|individuals, comprising nine senior independent academic representatives who are experts in
41|their field and two Alliance representatives. It will be Co-Chaired by Professors Rob Califf and
42|Rury Holman with other academic members comprising four further diabetologists and three
43|further cardiologists. Geographical balance will be sought. Decision making will be by
44|consensus.

observations.text: Main article reports random assignment to extended-release exenatide 2 mg or matching placebo weekly; defines primary composite first occurrence of cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, or nonfatal stroke; reports coprimary noninferiority/superiority hypotheses; and identifies EXSCEL as NCT01144338.
Participants were randomly assigned 1:1; the report describes computer-generated block randomization within each site, stratified by cardiovascular history.
Primary endpoint is first occurrence of cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, or nonfatal stroke in a time-to-event analysis.
Primary time-to-event analyses used Cox proportional hazards in ITT, defined as all randomized patients.
Primary ITT result: HR 0.91 (95% CI 0.83 to 1.00), noninferior for safety, not superior for efficacy.
Main article names EXSCEL ClinicalTrials.gov number NCT01144338; intake condition records registry query NCT01455896 unavailable. Identifier conflict is unresolved; no registry obtained.
